items.title: Skills for Claude Code and Codex
items.text:
This repo gives you a reusable sub-agent workflow for two tools:

  • Claude Code
  • Codex

The short version is simple:

  1. Install the skills from this repo.
  2. Run one setup script.
  3. Start working in your tool or target project.

items.title: Choose Your Path
items.text:
• Quick Start for the shortest setup steps
  • How to Use These Skills for the longer explanation
  • FAQ for common setup questions

items.title: What Is In This Repo
items.text:
• orchestrator-workflow/ for complex implementation tasks
  • refactor-workflow/ for refactoring tasks
  • claude-config/ for Claude-specific global config
  • codex/AGENTS.md for Codex project instructions
  • scripts/ for install helpers

items.title: When To Use This Repo
items.text:
Use this repo when:

  • you want the same orchestration style in Claude Code
  • you want Codex to work with a project-level AGENTS.md
  • you want a shared workflow layer that target projects can extend locally

items.title: Start Here
items.text: If you only need the practical steps, go to Quick Start.

items.title: Do I need both Claude and Codex?
items.text:
No. You can use only one path.

  • If you use Claude Code, install the skills and run ./scripts/install-claude-config.sh.
  • If you use Codex, install the skills and run ./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project.

items.title: Why are skills and Claude config separate steps?
items.text:
Because they do different jobs.

  • the skills add reusable workflow logic
  • the Claude config installs Claude-specific files into ~/.claude

For Claude, you usually want both.

items.title: Does Codex need claude-config/?
items.text:
No.

For Codex, the important pieces are:

  • the installed skills
  • AGENTS.md inside the target project

items.title: Do I run the scripts from my target project?
items.text:
No.

Clone this repo and run the scripts from this repo root.

Example:

cd /path/to/skills
./scripts/install-claude-config.sh
./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project

items.title: What does install-codex-agents.sh actually do?
items.text:
It copies the repository file codex/AGENTS.md into your target repo as AGENTS.md.

That file tells Codex how to use this orchestration workflow.

items.title: Why can Codex cost more than my previous Claude/ECC setup?
items.text:
Because the two environments do not expose the same routing model.

  • Claude + ECC has an explicit cost ladder with junior, middle, and senior roles, which makes cheapest-capable selection more predictable.
  • Codex can follow the same workflow shape, but cost control is often achieved through fewer delegations, shorter handoffs, and a tighter plan -> executor -> validation loop.

If Codex starts feeling expensive, the first thing to check is not only model choice but also whether the workflow is spawning unnecessary research or review steps.

items.title: What is the cheapest default behavior I should expect in Codex?
items.text:
The intended cheap default is:

  • quick plan
  • one executor
  • validation at the end

Research agents should be added only when missing facts block execution. Review agents should usually be added after implementation reaches a stable state.

items.title: Can my target project still have its own local rules?
items.text:
Yes.

This repo is the shared orchestration layer. Your target project can still define its own local roles and rules in AGENTS.md or .agents/**/SKILL.md.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text: Clone this repo first. Run the commands below from the repo root.

items.title: Claude
items.text:
1. Install Claude Code.
  2. Install the skills from this repo:
npx skills add <your-git-url-or-owner/repo> --skill '*' -g -a claude-code -y
  1. Run:
./scripts/install-claude-config.sh

Done:

  • Claude Code gets the reusable skills
  • the Claude config is copied into ~/.claude

items.title: Codex
items.text:
1. Install Codex.
  2. Install the skills from this repo:
npx skills add <your-git-url-or-owner/repo> --skill '*' -g -a codex -y
  1. Run:
./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project

Done:

  • Codex gets the reusable skills
  • your target repo gets an AGENTS.md file for this workflow

items.title: If You Use Both
items.text:
Install both skill targets at once:

npx skills add <your-git-url-or-owner/repo> --skill '*' -g -a claude-code -a codex -y

Then run:

./scripts/install-claude-config.sh
./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project

Use this when:

  • you want Claude to get the global config from claude-config/
  • you want Codex to get AGENTS.md inside a working project

items.title: What The Scripts Do
items.text:
./scripts/install-claude-config.sh

  • creates ~/.claude
  • copies CLAUDE.md
  • copies agents/, commands/, and output-styles/
  • installs statusline-command.sh

./scripts/install-codex-agents.sh /path/to/your/project

  • creates the target directory if needed
  • copies codex/AGENTS.md into that repo as AGENTS.md

items.title: How to Use These Skills
items.text:
This repo is meant to stay small and reusable.

It gives you:

  • shared orchestration skills
  • Claude-specific global config
  • Codex project instructions

items.title: The Main Idea
items.text:
There are two layers:

  1. Shared skills that both Claude Code and Codex can use
  2. Tool-specific setup for the tool you actually work with

That is why setup happens in two steps instead of one.

items.title: Claude Flow
items.text:
Claude uses:

  • installed skills from this repo
  • files copied into ~/.claude by ./scripts/install-claude-config.sh

This gives Claude the reusable workflow plus the Claude-specific global setup.

items.title: Codex Flow
items.text:
Codex uses:

  • installed skills from this repo
  • AGENTS.md inside the target repo

This gives Codex the reusable workflow plus project-level instructions.

items.title: How To Adapt This To Your Own Project
items.text:
Keep this repo focused on orchestration.

Put stack-specific roles in the target project, for example:

  • AGENTS.md
  • .agents/**/SKILL.md
  • project-specific rules files

The target repo should describe its own stack and domain. This repo should stay generic.

items.title: Recommended Reading Order
items.text:
If you are new to this repo:

  1. Read Quick Start
  2. Use the Claude or Codex path
  3. Come back here only if you need the longer explanation

items.title: Releases and dependency updates
items.text: This repository uses Release Please for versioning and changelog generation, and Renovate for pinned GitHub Actions updates.

items.title: Release flow
items.text:
1. Open pull requests with a Conventional Commit title. The scope is optional:
type(optional-scope): short summary
  1. Merge the pull request into main. The squash commit title must remain conventional.
  2. Release Please updates or opens a release pull request containing the next version and CHANGELOG.md entries.
  3. Merge the release pull request after its checks pass.
  4. Release Please creates the component-scoped skills-vX.Y.Z Git tag and GitHub release.

The manifest starts from a 0.0.0 baseline, while initial-version explicitly makes the first public release 0.1.0. The commit recorded as bootstrap-sha excludes earlier repository history from the first generated changelog. The simple release type is used because this repository has no package manifest; package-name and include-component-in-tag still provide component-scoped tags.

Release impact follows Conventional Commits:

  • fix(scope): ... and perf(scope): ... produce a patch release;
  • feat(scope): ... produces a minor release;
  • a breaking change marked with ! produces a major release;
  • docs, test, ci, build, refactor, and chore changes do not normally trigger a release by themselves, but can appear in the next generated changelog.

The PR Title workflow enforces the title format before merge. When squash merging, verify the final commit title in GitHub because Release Please reads merged commit history rather than the pull request body.

items.title: Renovate flow
items.text:
.github/renovate.json uses semantic chore(deps) commits, enables only the github-actions manager, and extends the shared public GitHub Actions preset. Renovate keeps immutable action SHAs current while preserving readable version comments.

The Renovate Config workflow runs:

  • when .github/renovate.json or its validation workflow changes;
  • weekly, to detect incompatibility with newer Renovate versions;
  • manually through workflow_dispatch.

It executes renovate-config-validator --strict .github/renovate.json. Renovate pull requests must pass the normal repository checks before merge. Major dependency updates still require explicit review; do not bypass branch protection or security review for an automated update.

items.title: Configuration files
items.text:
• release-please-config.json — release type, baseline, and changelog sections;
  • .release-please-manifest.json — last released version tracked by Release Please;
  • .github/workflows/release-please.yml — release PR and GitHub release automation;
  • .github/workflows/pr-title.yml — Conventional Commit title validation;
  • .github/renovate.json — semantic commit settings, enabled managers, grouping, and shared preset;
  • .github/workflows/renovate-config.yml — strict Renovate configuration validation.
